title: Classical economics

definition.text: Classical economics is the school of economic thought that flourished mainly in Britain from the late 18th to the mid-19th century, led by Adam Smith, David Ricardo, Thomas Malthus and John Stuart Mill.

facts.text: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations of 1776 is usually taken to mark its beginning.
The classical economists saw markets as largely self-regulating systems, a view captured by Smith's metaphor of the invisible hand.
Smith held that a nation's wealth is its yearly income, produced by labour, land and capital and shared out as wages, rent and profits.
They favoured free trade over the protectionism of the earlier mercantilists, and Ricardo explained trade's gains through comparative advantage.
John Stuart Mill believed a future 'stationary state' with constant population and capital was inevitable and desirable, an idea now called a steady-state economy.
From the 1870s it gave way to neoclassical economics, though many of its ideas remain fundamental.
Thomas Carlyle nicknamed it 'the dismal science', a jibe often linked to Malthus's gloomy analysis.

related: An Essay on the Principle of Population

title: Classical theory of value

definition.text: The classical theory of value explained prices by a 'natural price' set by lasting forces, toward which day-to-day market prices tend to move.

facts.text: William Petty first separated the market price, pushed about by passing influences, from the natural price.
Smith said market prices are drawn toward natural prices, somewhat like gravity.
For Smith the natural price was the sum of the natural rates of wages, profits and rent.
Petty held a land-and-labour theory of value, while the labour theory of value later clashed with Ricardo's comparative advantage.

contested_note: The theory of value, and how classical economics relates to neoclassical economics, are still debated.

definition.text: The conservation movement is an environmental, social and political movement that seeks to manage and protect natural resources, wild species and their habitats for the future.

facts.text: It grew from the practical need to keep up fisheries, wildlife, water, soil and forests.
It is often traced to John Evelyn's Sylva of 1662, which urged England to manage the rate of tree felling and replant cut trees.
Its 19th-century ethic held that human activity harms the environment, that there is a civic duty to keep it for future generations, and that science should guide that duty.
The first practical use of scientific conservation was in the forests of India in the mid-19th century.
It has broadened from sustainable yields of resources and wilderness preservation to the preservation of biodiversity.
Scholars note that early conservation often protected game for elite white hunters while policing hunting by Indigenous and poor people.
